speakers: David Harding (Adam, Harding and Lueck Ltd)
summary: Question: do mathematical models in finance have enough empirical grounding, and how should one test them. Method: philosophical essay on scientific method, Adam Smith and efficient market theory (OCR of 1994 Phil. Trans. R. Soc. paper, no data). Conclusion: models must be falsifiable and tested by trading against the market; speculation based on empirical observation is the productive path.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: of the sufficiency of the empirical grounding of such models to the task of drawing useful inferences about such a reality; and of the danger of unwittingly propagating erroneous conclusions about this reality in the absence of such a grounding.
claims.claim: Paper's aim: examine whether mathematical models in finance have enough empirical grounding to support useful inference, and warn that models lacking such grounding spread erroneous conclusions; suggests how to enrich empirical grounding.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: the theory cannot be the reality ; it can at best only be a near perfect simulation of that reality.
claims.claim: A model can never be the reality, only a simulation of it; even a model matching all known observations cannot be called true because the universe of observations keeps expanding.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: such a model must be capable of producing empirically falsifiable predictions and must thus be capable of being subjected to an unbiased test of its value within its own conceptual framework.
claims.claim: Models must make empirically falsifiable predictions testable without bias; a theory's utility is the quality of its predictions and their accord with observation.
claims.exact_rule: accept a model only if it yields falsifiable predictions tested against empirical observation; judge by predictive accuracy
claims.direction: judge models on out-of-sample predictive utility

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: it would not be logically correct to infer that mathematics is reality, that the elegant solution is necessarily the best.
claims.claim: Mathematical elegance is an aesthetic criterion and does not imply a model is correct; the best model is not necessarily the elegant one.
claims.conditions: Directed at mathematicians working in finance

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: The idea that models are nearly true or are true for all practical purposes must be rejected as forcefully as the idea that they are true.
claims.claim: Models should not be treated as 'true for all practical purposes': Newtonian mechanics looked sufficient until a tiny discrepancy with observation opened the way to Einstein, so small unexplained deviations matter.
claims.conditions: Illustrated by Newton-Einstein example (a tiny inconsistency had enormous consequences)

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: If they look true we must look for the explanation.
claims.claim: When a model appears to fit, the explanation for why it looks true should be investigated rather than accepted.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: A theory like yours, founded on the nature of man, which is always the same, will last, when those that are founded upon his opinions, which are always changing, will and must be forgotten.
claims.claim: Edmund Burke (1759 letter to Adam Smith, cited): theories based on unchanging human nature last, whereas theories based on changing opinions are forgotten.
claims.conditions: Cited as support that durable models rest on human nature

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Natural science provides an independent method of arbitration between views
claims.claim: Empirical testing gives an independent way to arbitrate between views, replacing sterile conflict with constructive argument.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: in economics as in other social sciences, progress has been held back by the sheer practical difficulty of employing the experimental method.
claims.claim: Economics progresses slowly because controlled experiments on society are rarely possible and the subject has a mind of its own; historical 'experiments' are slow and less conclusive.
claims.conditions: Social science object of study responds to the models

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Smith’s models did give rise to empirically testable, interesting and often counter-intuitive predictions about the world and which in the messy social laboratory of the past three centuries have received far more support than contradiction.
claims.claim: Adam Smith's market model is presented as a scientific theory with empirically testable predictions that three centuries of history have mostly supported.
claims.conditions: Smith cited as example of deeply empirical model construction

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: Had Smith lived through the subsequent centuries there would have been many occasions on which he would have been able to profit handsomely by exploiting the difference between his theories’ predictions and the common opinion
claims.claim: Ultimate test of a model's utility is profit from exploiting differences between its predictions and common opinion; older models are easier to judge because social systems evolve slowly.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: In economics and the study of markets there can be no more incorruptible measure of utility than profit accrued by arbitraging the predictions of a model against the common view (the market).
claims.claim: Profit from trading a model's predictions against the market is the most honest test of its scientific utility; beating the market is thus an empirical test, not mere greed.
claims.exact_rule: validate models by trading profit relative to market consensus
claims.direction: use realised trading profit as the test of a model

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: And a study of speculation will show that most successful speculators can be well described as ‘observers’.
claims.claim: Successful speculators are detached, unemotional observers; speculating is the empirical scientist's way of testing theories.

claims.speaker: David Harding
claims.quote: The various versions of the theory begin essentially by asserting that it is impossible to make money by applying mathematical modelling to the science of speculation.
claims.claim: Efficient market theory, in effect, asserts that modelling cannot make money; its price prediction is the uninteresting null (no better estimate of tomorrow's price than today's).

claims.claim: The efficient-market claim that returns come from a known distribution with estimable parameters appears falsified: returns in all markets are non-parametric and non-stationary (links to his later Sharpe-ratio critique).

reasoning.question: What is the scientific status of mathematical models in finance (especially efficient market theory), and how should their usefulness be judged?

thesis.statement: Financial models should be judged like natural-science models by the falsifiable predictions they make, and the most honest test is trading profit against the market; by that standard efficient market theory has limited scientific utility, and empirical speculation is the intellectual front line.

foundations.premise: Models are never reality; their value is the utility of their falsifiable predictions.
Markets are made of agents with minds, and controlled experiments are impossible.
Return processes are non-parametric and non-stationary.
Theories grounded in stable human nature endure.

reasoning.forward_looking_inputs: (reader) No specific inputs. The method says any signal should be a falsifiable prediction against market-implied expectations, validated on data after the model was frozen; signals grounded in stable human behaviour should last longer than those grounded in transient opinions.
reader_inferences: (reader) The "judge models developed some time ago without prior knowledge" principle is the case for a frozen-rules holdout test.
(reader) The Burke quote suggests behavioural (human-nature) anomalies such as trend are more durable than opinion-driven ones.
(reader) Profit as test needs a significance standard to separate skill from luck, which the paper does not provide.
